newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Britain showers HK stalwarts with farewell honours.
newsitem.headline: Britain showers HK stalwarts with farewell honours.

text.p: Britain has showered knighthoods and other awards on a galaxy of Hong Kong stalwarts in Queen Elizabeth's annual Birthday Honours just two weeks before the colony is handed over to China.

Financial Secretary Donald Tsang, a colourful character known for his cautious fiscal polices, liberal political views and gaudy bowties, topped the local honours list earning a knighthood for his contribution to Hong Kong's public life.
He will be known as Sir Donald Tsang.

Heir to the throne Prince Charles will hand out the honours in a colourful investiture ceremony on June 29 in Government House, a stately mansion on the slopes of Hong Kong Island which is the official residence of colonial Governor Chris Patten.
Charles is coming to Hong Kong to hand back the 156-year-old colony to China, from which it was wrested in the gunboat diplomacy linked to the 19th century opium trade wars.
The prince will be co-presiding over a glitzy joint handover ceremony on the spectacular Hong Kong seafront with China's President Jiang Zemin, at midnight on June 30.
Also knighted in the swansong honours was Jimmy McGregor, a member of Patten's cabinet, a former lawmaker and businessman, and a long-term stalwart of the colony's commerce chambers.

Tycoon Gordon Wu, chairman of Hong Kong conglomerate Hopewell Holdings, which has been a big player in the infrastructure business in China and southeast Asia, picked up Hong Kong's third knighthood in the list.
Many senior government officials and the supporters of the governor were also honoured.
Tsang, 53, in 1995 became the first Chinese to fill the post of Financial Secretary in a century and a half of colonial rule.
The job was previously the exclusive domain of expatriates.
Tsang has been reappointed by the post-colonial leader Tung Chee-hwa, who takes over from Patten on July 1.

Respected by the business community in the territory and abroad, Tsang is seen as a man who can keep Hong Kong's fiscal and financial policies on an even keel in a sensitive time as Hong Kong adjusts to life as an autonomous region of China.
"He represents what the markets are looking for. It's not so much Tung or Jiang Zemin, it's Donald Tsang that people want to hear," a stock market trader said.

However, one analyst said the knighthood might tip the balance of favour against Tsang because China is deeply suspicious of those applauded by the Patten regime, and that it might mean Tsang would not be staying long in his job.
The analyst noted Tsang had been outspoken against his future boss's plan to curb civil and political liberties.
While many senior officials were rewarded, one significant missing name was Chief Secretary Anson Chan, Patten's deputy and head of Hong Kong's Civil Service, who was not knighted.
Chan has also been reappointed by Tung.
It is no secret in Hong Kong political circles that she has effectively been told by Britain she can have a knighthood when she wants it, in reward for her long service and loyalty.

Chan is well aware, however, that a British knighthood would be frowned upon by China and could spell the end of her career and kill the opportunity to influence the new government by working inside the system, sources close to her said.

Other honoured civil servants included Security Secretary Peter Lai, Constitutional Affairs Secretary Nicholas Ng, Planning And Environment Secretary Bowen Leung, Transport Secretary Gordon Siu and Police Chief Eddie Hui, as Commanders of the Most Excellent Order of the British Empire (CBE).
Patten's personal adviser Martin Dinham was named a CBE, while his colleague Edward Llewellyn received a Member of the Most Excellent Order of the British Empire (MBE).
Patten's feisty spokesman Kerry McGlynn, an Australian, became an Officer of the Most Excellent Order of the British Empire (OBE).
